sections.changelog:
Changed

  • **The suggestions dropdown fetches its results in one go.** Shaping a suggestion reads a title, a link, a picture and a price, and each row started from an uncached post — on a cache miss, two queries per suggestion. The whole set is now fetched at once, on both paths that build the dropdown, including the one that offers best-sellers when nothing matched, where the cache is coldest. The results page is unaffected: it never goes through this route.
  • **The exact-match pass no longer builds a product object per result.** Checking the first hundred results for a title or article number that equals the query loaded a full WooCommerce product for each of them, and every one of those cost two queries — two hundred on a single search, for two short strings. The whole head is now fetched in one go and the article number read from the same meta WooCommerce's own data store reads it from; posts and pages skip the article check altogether, which for them never had an answer. Measured on a 14 700-product catalogue: 216 ms and 220 queries became 12 ms and one, and the results are unchanged. A store that filters article numbers through `woocommerce_product_get_sku` no longer sees that filter here — worth checking before updating if the store has one.
  • **Stock is read from WooCommerce's own product table instead of the meta table.** Ranking joined `wp_postmeta` for a single out-of-stock flag, and that table indexes a post but not the pairing of a post with a meta key — so every candidate row cost a scan of the ~17 meta rows the product carries. WooCommerce keeps the same value on a primary key in its product lookup table, written from the same meta. Measured on a 14 700-product catalogue: the ranking query fell from 144 to 51 ms where out-of-stock products are pushed down, and from 198 to 68 ms where they are hidden — with the result set, order included, identical row for row. The category badges read the same source, so the number under a category still matches what a click on it opens.
  • **The "?" sits on the middle of its line.** It hung from a fixed two-pixel drop below the baseline, which put it 2.5px below the centre of the section line it belongs to — enough to read as an afterthought stuck onto the end of the text. It is now centred against the line itself, so it holds its place whatever font and size a theme gives the section line.
  • **The tick and the count line up with the category name, not with the middle of the row.** Since a value carries a second line naming its section, centring the checkbox against the whole row pushed it into the gap between the two lines — it read as belonging to neither. Both now sit on the name's own baseline, so the eye follows one line across the row whether the value has a section line or not.
  • **The panel's button says "Apply" instead of "Apply filters".** In a sidebar column the longer wording wrapped onto two lines and made the button twice as tall as the row above it; the heading over the values already says what is being applied.

Fixed

  • **A title with a quote, an apostrophe or a dash can now match the query exactly.** The exact-match check compared the query against the *rendered* title, which WordPress runs through its typographic filter: in a Russian locale `"Премиум"` comes back as `«Премиум»` and ` - ` as `—`. Stripping punctuation for the comparison then left the digits of those entities in the key, so the two strings could never be equal — a shopper pasting such a title in full got everything except a guaranteed first place. The comparison now uses the stored title, which is also what the index is built from. Affects 8.4% of titles on a 14 700-product catalogue and 4.1% on a 13 000-product one; in practice the product was usually first on relevance alone, so the visible change is small.
